name: Wind waves
summary: Most ocean waves are made by wind transferring energy to the water surface.
how: Wind friction creates capillary ripples, which give the wind more grip; waves grow with wind speed, duration and fetch (distance). Water particles move in circles, so energy travels but water mostly stays in place. Waves break when height exceeds about one-seventh of the wavelength or when they reach depths of ~1.3 times their height.
where: Everywhere; the biggest under the Southern Ocean westerlies.
effects: Shape beaches and coasts, mix the upper ocean, drive surf.
data: Significant wave height is measured by buoys and satellite altimeters; ~30 m waves have been recorded in storms.

name: Ripples (capillary waves)
summary: The tiniest waves, controlled by surface tension rather than gravity.
how: When wind first touches calm water, surface tension acts as a restoring force, making ripples shorter than ~1.7 cm. They give later waves a rougher surface to grow on. Sand ripples on the seabed form separately as currents and waves move sand grains.
where: Any water surface, and sandy seabeds.
effects: Start the wave-growth process; sand ripples record past currents in rocks.
data: Ripple speed is a minimum (~23 cm/s) at ~1.7 cm wavelength.

name: Swell
summary: Waves that have left the storm that made them and travel across ocean basins.
how: Long-period waves outrun short ones and sort themselves into smooth swell, losing little energy over thousands of km.
where: Southern Ocean storms send swell to Hawaii and California.
effects: Surf, coastal erosion, ship motion.
data: Swell periods of 15–25 s.

name: Rogue waves
summary: Unexpectedly huge waves more than twice the surrounding wave height.
how: Waves add together constructively, and nonlinear focusing can pile energy into one giant wave; currents opposing waves (e.g. Agulhas) increase risk.
effects: Sink or damage ships.
data: The Draupner wave (1995, 25.6 m) was the first measured; the Ucluelet wave (2020) was nearly 3× the background.

name: Tsunamis
summary: Long waves set off by sudden seafloor movement, landslides or volcanoes.
how: An earthquake lifts the seafloor and the water above it. In deep water the wave is low but travels at ~700–800 km/h; near shore it slows and grows tall.
where: Pacific Ring of Fire, Indian Ocean (Sunda Trench), Mediterranean.
effects: The 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami killed ~230,000; Tōhoku 2011 killed ~18,000.
data: DART buoys detect pressure changes on the seabed.

name: Tides
summary: The regular rise and fall of the sea caused by the Moon and Sun.
how: The Moon's gravity pulls water into two bulges; Earth spins under them. Spring tides occur at new and full moon when Sun and Moon align; neap tides at quarter moons. Coastline shape amplifies tides.
where: Everywhere; largest in the Bay of Fundy (~16 m); India's Gulf of Khambhat has ~11 m.
effects: Intertidal habitats, tidal power, navigation.
data: Tide gauges since the 1800s also track sea-level rise.

name: Tidal bores
summary: A wall of water that travels up a river as the tide floods in.
how: A large tidal range funnelled into a narrowing estuary.
effects: Dangerous for boats; surfed by enthusiasts.
data: Qiantang bore reaches ~9 m.

name: Tropical cyclones
summary: Hurricanes, typhoons and cyclones are giant storms powered by warm ocean water.
how: Sea surface above ~26.5°C fuels evaporation; rising moist air releases heat as it condenses, lowering pressure and drawing in more air. Earth's rotation (Coriolis effect) makes it spin, so cyclones cannot form at the equator. Low wind shear lets the vertical structure build. An eye forms where air sinks at the centre.
effects: Wind, storm surge, flooding rain; a warmer ocean makes the strongest storms stronger and wetter.
data: About 80–90 tropical cyclones form each year worldwide.

name: Storm surge
summary: The rise in sea level pushed ashore by a storm's winds and low pressure.
how: Onshore winds pile water against the coast; low pressure lifts the sea ~1 cm per hPa; shallow funnel-shaped bays amplify it.
where: Bay of Bengal, Gulf of Mexico, North Sea.
effects: The 1970 Bhola cyclone surge killed ~300,000 in Bangladesh.
data: Surges can exceed 8 m.

name: Monsoon
summary: A seasonal reversal of winds that brings the rainy season to South Asia and beyond.
how: In summer, land heats faster than the ocean, creating low pressure that draws moist ocean air inland; in winter the pattern reverses.
where: Indian Ocean, Asia, West Africa, Australia.
effects: India receives ~70–80% of its rainfall from the southwest monsoon.
data: Onset over Kerala around 1 June.

name: El Niño and La Niña (ENSO)
summary: The biggest natural swing in Earth's climate, centred on the tropical Pacific.
how: Normally trade winds push warm water west. In El Niño they weaken, warm water spreads east and upwelling off Peru shuts down; La Niña strengthens the normal state.
effects: El Niño raises global temperature, brings drought to India and Australia and floods to Peru; triggers coral bleaching.
data: Tracked with the Oceanic Niño Index.

name: Indian Ocean Dipole
summary: A see-saw of sea temperature between the western and eastern Indian Ocean.
how: Positive phase: warmer west, cooler east; negative is the reverse.
effects: Positive IOD boosts Indian monsoon rains and East African floods; drives Australian droughts and fires (2019).
data: Dipole Mode Index.

name: Upwelling
summary: Cold, nutrient-rich deep water rising to the surface, fuelling the richest fisheries.
how: Along-shore winds plus Earth's rotation push surface water offshore (Ekman transport), and deep water rises to replace it.
where: Peru, California, Benguela, Canary, Somalia, Kerala.
effects: Upwelling zones cover ~1% of the ocean but give ~20% of the fish catch.
data: Seen as cold, green water in satellite images.

name: Ocean gyres
summary: Huge rotating current systems in each ocean basin.
how: Driven by trade winds and westerlies plus the Coriolis effect, with fast western boundary currents (Gulf Stream, Kuroshio).
effects: Concentrate floating plastic (the 'garbage patches').
data: The North Atlantic Gyre encloses the Sargasso Sea.

name: Thermohaline circulation
summary: The global conveyor belt driven by differences in temperature and salt.
how: Cold, salty water sinks in the North Atlantic and around Antarctica, spreads through the deep ocean, and slowly rises elsewhere.
effects: Distributes heat, oxygen and carbon; the AMOC is its Atlantic branch.
data: Water takes ~1,000 years to complete a circuit.

name: Ekman transport and the Coriolis effect
summary: Why ocean currents turn right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern.
how: Earth's rotation deflects moving water; wind-driven surface layers move at an angle to the wind, net transport 90° to it.
effects: Explains upwelling, gyres and cyclone spin.
data: Named after Walfrid Ekman (1905).

name: Rip currents
summary: Narrow, fast currents flowing away from the beach.
how: Breaking waves pile water on shore; it escapes seaward through gaps in sandbars.
effects: The leading surf-beach hazard; swim parallel to shore to escape.
data: Speeds up to ~2.5 m/s.

name: Internal waves
summary: Huge waves inside the ocean between layers of different density.
how: Tides flowing over ridges disturb density layers, making waves that can be 100 m+ high but invisible at the surface.
where: South China Sea (largest known), Andaman Sea, Strait of Gibraltar.
effects: Mix the ocean, move nutrients, affect submarines.
data: Visible from space as surface slicks.

name: Ocean eddies
summary: Swirling whirlpools of water that break off from currents.
how: Instabilities in strong currents pinch off rings of warm or cold water.
where: Everywhere, especially near Gulf Stream, Agulhas and Kuroshio.
effects: Carry heat, nutrients and larvae; Agulhas rings leak Indian Ocean water into the Atlantic.
data: Tracked by satellite altimetry.

name: Whirlpools and maelstroms
summary: Powerful rotating tidal currents.
how: Strong tides flowing through narrow straits create vortices.
effects: Navigation hazards and legends.
data: Saltstraumen currents reach ~40 km/h.

name: Marine heatwaves
summary: Periods of unusually warm ocean water, now becoming more frequent and intense.
how: Weak winds, high pressure and ocean heat build-up allow surface water to stay abnormally warm.
where: Global; e.g. the 2014–16 'Blob', the 2023 North Atlantic heatwave.
effects: Coral bleaching, kelp loss, seabird and fish die-offs.
data: Have roughly doubled in frequency since the 1980s.

name: Sea-level rise
summary: Global sea level is rising as ice melts and warming water expands.
how: Thermal expansion plus melting glaciers and ice sheets; local land subsidence adds to it.
where: Global; fastest relative rise in sinking deltas.
effects: Coastal flooding, saltwater intrusion, threat to atoll nations.
data: ~21 cm since 1900, accelerating to over 4 mm a year.

name: Sea ice formation
summary: How the polar oceans freeze and why it matters.
how: Seawater freezes at about −1.8°C; ice crystals form frazil and pancake ice that consolidate. Salt is rejected, making dense water that sinks.
effects: Habitat for algae, krill, seals and bears; reflects sunlight; drives deep-water formation.
data: Satellite records since 1979.

name: The water cycle and the ocean
summary: The ocean is the source of most rain and the end of most rivers.
how: About 86% of global evaporation comes from the ocean; most falls back over the sea, the rest over land, returning via rivers and groundwater.
effects: Drives weather; ocean salinity patterns record the cycle intensifying with warming.
data: About 1.3 billion km³ of water are in the ocean, ~97% of Earth's water.

name: Dead zones (hypoxia)
summary: Areas where oxygen is too low for most marine life.
how: Nutrient runoff fuels algal blooms; bacteria decomposing them use up oxygen in stratified water.
where: Gulf of Mexico, Baltic, Arabian Sea, Chesapeake Bay.
effects: Over 500 coastal dead zones are known.
data: Gulf of Mexico dead zone averages ~14,000 km².

name: Harmful algal blooms (red tides)
summary: Explosive growth of toxic algae that discolour the water.
how: Warm water, nutrients and calm conditions favour blooms of dinoflagellates and diatoms.
effects: Fish kills, shellfish poisoning, respiratory irritation.
data: Karenia brevis blooms in Florida.

name: Bioluminescent bays and milky seas
summary: Glowing waters caused by light-producing plankton and bacteria.
how: Dinoflagellates flash when disturbed; 'milky seas' are vast areas lit steadily by bacteria (Vibrio).
where: Puerto Rico's Mosquito Bay, Maldives, Indian coasts; milky seas in the Arabian Sea and Indonesia.
effects: Tourism; milky seas are seen by satellite.
data: A 2019 milky sea covered ~100,000 km².

name: Waterspouts
summary: Rotating columns of air and mist over water.
how: Fair-weather waterspouts form under developing cumulus; tornadic ones descend from thunderstorms.
effects: Hazard to boats.
data: Typically last 5–10 minutes.

name: Hydrothermal plumes
summary: Clouds of mineral-laden hot water rising from seafloor vents.
how: Seawater heated by magma rises and mixes, spreading metals and nutrients for hundreds of km.
effects: Supply iron to the ocean.
data: Plumes detected over 4,000 km from vents.

name: Turbidity currents
summary: Underwater avalanches of sediment racing down slopes.
how: Earthquakes or floods destabilise sediment that flows downslope faster than the water.
effects: Broke transatlantic cables in 1929 (Grand Banks); carry microplastics to the deep.
data: Speeds up to ~70 km/h.

name: Brinicles
summary: 'Icicles of death' growing down from sea ice into the water.
how: Cold, salty brine leaking from sea ice freezes seawater around it as it sinks.
effects: Can trap and freeze bottom-dwelling animals.
data: First filmed in 2011.
